title: Principles of Green Chemistry
description: Twelve rules for chemistry that doesn't ruin the planet

concepts.title: The Twelve Principles
concepts.contentHtml:
Anastas and Warner formalized green chemistry's Twelve Principles in 1998. The headlines: prevent waste rather than treat it after; design safer products and synthesis; use renewable feedstocks; design for degradation; use catalysis; minimize energy.

Each principle is a design constraint. Together they reframe chemistry from 'make the molecule' to 'make the molecule with the smallest possible footprint.'

The principles aren't laws of nature — they're heuristics for synthesis decisions. Even partial application can dramatically reduce waste.

concepts.title: Atom Economy
concepts.contentHtml:
Atom economy measures what fraction of all reactant atoms end up in the desired product. AE = (mass of product) / (sum of masses of all reactants) × 100%.

Traditional Wittig olefination has terrible atom economy — most of the phosphorus reagent is wasted as triphenylphosphine oxide. The Diels-Alder reaction has 100% atom economy — every atom in the reactants ends up in the product.

High atom economy isn't always achievable but is a powerful design heuristic. It often correlates with cleaner, cheaper, more practical chemistry.

concepts.title: E-Factor
concepts.contentHtml:
The E-factor (Sheldon, 1992) is mass of waste / mass of product. Bulk chemicals: ~1 (good). Fine chemicals: ~50. Pharmaceuticals: ~100-1000. Total industry footprint: hundreds of millions of tonnes per year of waste, mostly aqueous and solvent.

The pharmaceutical industry has been a particularly enthusiastic adopter of green chemistry, partly because their E-factors are so embarrassing.

title: Solvents — The Hidden Footprint
description: Often most of the waste is the solvent

concepts.title: The Solvent Problem
concepts.contentHtml:
Solvents typically account for 80-90% of the mass used in pharmaceutical manufacturing — and most of the waste. Many are toxic (chlorinated solvents like dichloromethane, chloroform), volatile (ozone-depleting CFCs were once standard), or both.

Reducing or replacing problematic solvents is one of the highest-impact green chemistry interventions. The solvent guides like ETH Zurich's chart classes solvents by safety/health/environmental score.

concepts.title: Greener Alternatives
concepts.contentHtml:
Water is the ultimate green solvent — cheap, non-toxic, non-flammable. Many reactions thought impossible in water are now routine — 'on-water' catalysis exploits hydrophobic effects.

Supercritical CO₂ dissolves many organics, is non-toxic, and the solvent recovers itself when pressure is released. Used industrially for caffeine extraction from coffee.

Ionic liquids and deep eutectic solvents have negligible vapor pressure and are tunable for specific reactions. Their environmental profile depends sensitively on the cation/anion choice — not all are obviously 'green.'

concepts.title: Solvent-Free Synthesis
concepts.contentHtml:
The greenest solvent is no solvent. Mechanochemistry — grinding solid reactants in a mill — drives many reactions cleanly with zero solvent waste.

The IUPAC named mechanochemistry one of the top 10 emerging chemistries in 2019. Pharmaceutical co-crystals, MOFs, and inorganic materials are increasingly made by milling.

Neat reactions (mixing pure liquids) and solid-state reactions also avoid solvent. They're not always feasible, but when they are, the gains are dramatic.

title: Catalysis
description: Why catalysts are nature's gift to green chemistry

concepts.title: Why Catalysis Is Green
concepts.contentHtml:
A catalyst speeds a reaction without being consumed. Compared to stoichiometric reagents, catalysts are used in tiny amounts, lowering waste enormously.

They also let you avoid harsh conditions — hot, high-pressure forcing chemistry can often be replaced by mild catalysis. Lower energy, less side reactions, less waste.

Catalyst design is now a central tool of green chemistry. The Nobel for Sharpless asymmetric oxidation (2001) and click chemistry (2022) both reflect catalysis-driven advances.

concepts.title: Heterogeneous vs Homogeneous
concepts.contentHtml:
Heterogeneous catalysts (solid catalyst, liquid or gas reactants) are easy to separate from products — just filter or decant. The Haber-Bosch process for ammonia uses iron; refineries crack hydrocarbons over zeolites.

Homogeneous catalysts (dissolved in the same phase) are typically more selective and tunable, but harder to recover. Transition-metal-organic complexes drive most modern asymmetric synthesis.

Combining the two — heterogenized homogeneous catalysts on supports — gets the best of both. Active research area.

concepts.title: Biocatalysis
concepts.contentHtml:
Enzymes are nature's catalysts — exquisite selectivity, mild conditions (room temperature, water, neutral pH), often single-enantiomer products.

Biocatalysis uses isolated enzymes or whole cells. Frances Arnold's Nobel (2018) was for directed evolution — using natural selection in the lab to evolve enzymes for non-natural substrates.

Industrial biocatalysis now produces sitagliptin (a diabetes drug), some statins, and many flavors and fragrances. Often it competes — and beats — chemical synthesis on cost and yield.

concepts.title: From Petrochemicals to Biorefinery
concepts.contentHtml:
Most synthetic organic chemicals trace their lineage to petroleum. Green chemistry asks: can we replace fossil feedstocks with renewable ones?

A biorefinery processes biomass (corn, sugarcane, wood, agricultural waste) into chemical building blocks. Bio-ethanol, lactic acid, succinic acid, and 5-HMF are widely produced from biomass.

Cellulosic biomass (corn stover, switchgrass, wood) is more sustainable than food crops, but harder to break down. Enzyme-mediated saccharification has improved dramatically over the last decade.

concepts.title: Bio-Based Polymers
concepts.contentHtml:
Polylactic acid (PLA) from corn-derived lactic acid is now produced at hundreds of thousands of tonnes per year. PHA polyesters from microbial fermentation are biodegradable bioplastics.

Bio-based monomers don't have to make biodegradable polymers — bio-PE (polyethylene from sugarcane ethanol) is chemically identical to fossil-PE but has a much lower carbon footprint over its life cycle.

Drop-in replacements that match incumbent polymer properties accelerate adoption. New bio-derived molecules with novel properties are an active research frontier.

concepts.title: Carbon Capture as Feedstock
concepts.contentHtml:
Most ambitious of all: use atmospheric or flue-gas CO₂ directly as a chemical building block. Methanol, urea, and polycarbonates are already made from CO₂ at industrial scale, and the field is growing rapidly.

The thermodynamics is hard — CO₂ is the lowest-energy carbon form, so you need energy input. But coupling to renewable electricity (electrocatalytic CO₂ reduction) closes the loop: solar electrons + CO₂ + H₂O → fuels and chemicals.

Solar-fuel research is a Nobel-anticipating frontier in this area.

title: Industrial Practice & Frontier
description: Where green chemistry actually shows up

concepts.title: Industrial Adoption
concepts.contentHtml:
Green chemistry has been quietly transformative in pharma. Pfizer's sertraline (Zoloft) synthesis was redesigned to cut waste by ~80% and energy use ~60% — a Presidential Green Chemistry Award winner.

Bulk chemicals have improved, too: many heavy-metal catalysts replaced with milder alternatives, dichloromethane replaced with greener solvents in many industrial routes.

Driver: cost. Less waste means less raw material, less workup, less disposal. Green chemistry often saves money once the redesign cost is amortized.

concepts.title: Life Cycle Assessment
concepts.contentHtml:
A truly green process must be evaluated end-to-end. Life cycle assessment (LCA) tracks environmental impact across raw materials, manufacturing, use, and disposal.

Sometimes 'green' chemistry isn't: a bio-based feedstock requiring vast water and land, or a recyclable polymer needing energy-intensive separation. LCA reveals these tradeoffs quantitatively.

Standardized LCA methods (ISO 14040 series) underpin much corporate sustainability reporting. They're imperfect but indispensable.

concepts.title: Frontiers
concepts.contentHtml:
Photocatalysis using visible light is advancing fast — sunlight as a reagent. Electrocatalysis can replace stoichiometric oxidants with electrons.

Continuous flow chemistry replaces batch reactors with small, integrated, high-efficiency systems — easier to control, lower waste, better safety. Many pharmaceutical companies have built flow capabilities for key steps.

Closing chemical loops, designing molecules for end-of-life, and using AI for retrosynthesis prediction are reshaping how chemistry is practiced. Green chemistry is no longer a niche — it's becoming the way chemistry is done.
